videoIdeas.title: Speak like you mean it
videoIdeas.hook: You don't have a confidence problem. You have a conviction problem.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is one of my three pillars but not a single post in my top 15 actually teaches it — it's all commentary. Meanwhile @lifeofdinoo_ and @birdtart01 are pulling 50k-780k on practical 'how to communicate' breakdowns (small talk, networking questions). There's an obvious gap here I'm leaving on the table.
videoIdeas.script:
You don't have a confidence problem. You have a conviction problem.

Watch someone nervous speak. They rush, they trail off, they apologise before they've even said anything. That's not shyness. That's someone who doesn't fully believe the thing they're about to say.

Because when you actually believe something, you slow down. You let the silence sit. You're not begging the room to agree with you.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, was described as speaking so clearly that if you counted his words, you could. He didn't spray. He weighed every sentence.

So stop practising your voice in the mirror. Go and become certain about what you're saying. The delivery fixes itself once the belief is there.

visuals.setting: Plain wall or bookshelf, mid-shot, sitting or standing still. Muted tones, calm energy — you're the composed one in the room. Minimal hand movement to model the point.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a hard cut to your face already talking, dead still, with on-screen text: 'confidence ≠ conviction'.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open of you deliberately pausing in silence for 2 seconds before the first line lands
Split-screen: a rushed nervous speaker vs you speaking slowly, text 'spot the difference'
On-screen text punchline that stays: 'nervous = you don't believe it yet'

videoIdeas.title: Al-Qawi wal-Ameen
videoIdeas.hook: Everyone wants to be followed. Almost nobody wants to be trustworthy first.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Prophetic-leadership post (Al-Qawi wal-Ameen, 11 qualities) did 508 views with strong 58 likes — good ratio, under-distributed. This is squarely my leadership pillar and it's the content that separates me from generic commentary. @doctordaanish proved character-based content scales (193k on 'good character is built at home'). Turn my leadership framework into a repeatable series.
videoIdeas.script:
Everyone wants to be followed. Almost nobody wants to be trustworthy first.

The Quran gives you the order in two words: Al-Qawi wal-Ameen. Strong, and trustworthy. In that sequence.

We've flipped it. We chase the strength — the following, the influence, the platform — and we'll sort out the character later. Later never comes.

Here's the test. Would the people closest to you, the ones who see you off-camera, vouch for your character? Not your talent. Your character.

If the answer's shaky, you're not building a leader. You're building a fraud with good lighting.

Get trustworthy first. The strength means nothing without it.

visuals.setting: Clean, slightly more formal — collared shirt, neutral background. Steady mid-shot, low energy but firm. This is the 'sit down, I'm telling you something that matters' tone.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'strong AND trustworthy — in that order' appears word by word as you say the first line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open: hold up two fingers, 'two words, and we got the order wrong'
Pattern interrupt — start with 'your character is failing a test you don't know you're taking'
Text-only opening frame with the two Arabic words before you appear

videoIdeas.title: High agency isn't a personality
videoIdeas.hook: Stop calling it luck. You just watched someone take action while you scrolled.
videoIdeas.rationale: @birdtart01 got 57k on 'how to develop high agency' with almost no substance — just the promise. This concept is trending in the self-dev space and I can actually give it depth with an Islamic frame, which none of my competitors do. Mindset is a core pillar and my current mindset content is thin.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop calling it luck. You just watched someone take action while you scrolled.

High agency isn't a personality trait you're born with. It's a decision you make about forty times a day. The problem lands, and you either ask 'what can I do' or you ask 'why is this happening to me'.

One of those questions moves you. The other just feels productive.

And for us there's no excuse to sit in the second one. Tawakkul was never 'do nothing and wait'. Tie your camel, then trust. The tying is your job.

So the next time something breaks, catch yourself before you complain. Ask the better question. Do the small thing you can actually do right now. That's the whole skill. Repeated.

visuals.setting: Walking-and-talking outdoors, or a dynamic indoor space — slightly higher energy than the others to match 'action'. Natural light, moving.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-stride, already mid-sentence, on-screen text: 'high agency, explained properly'.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: phone in hand scrolling, then look up at camera 'this is the problem'
On-screen text of the two questions side by side, one crossed out
Quick jump-cut between 'why me' and 'what now' as the words are said

videoIdeas.title: Winning the argument, losing the point
videoIdeas.hook: You can be completely right and still be the reason nobody listened.
videoIdeas.rationale: My highest-engagement posts are commentary and refutations (protests post: 6,134 views; sectarianism: 24 comments). That audience is here for how I argue. This turns my natural subject matter into a public-speaking lesson — composure under fire — which is a pillar I under-serve, and ties directly to what already works for me.
videoIdeas.script:
You can be completely right and still be the reason nobody listened.

I see it constantly online. Someone has the correct point, the evidence, everything — and they deliver it with so much venom that the other person digs in harder. Congratulations. You won the argument and lost the human.

The skill isn't landing the point. It's landing it in a way the other person can actually receive.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, dealt with open hostility with a composure we can't even imagine. Not because he was weak — because losing his composure would've cost him the message.

So when you're right, slow down. Lower your voice, not your standard. Being loud and being convincing are not the same thing. Learn the difference before you open your mouth.

visuals.setting: Calm indoor setup, seated, deliberately still and quiet to embody 'composure'. Contrast your calm delivery against the heated topic.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'right + loud = ignored' while you sit completely still and start low.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open whispering the first line, forcing viewers to turn volume up
Pattern interrupt: raise voice for one word then immediately drop it, 'see how that felt?'
Text punchline held on screen: 'won the argument, lost the human'

videoIdeas.title: Outrage is not action
videoIdeas.hook: Reposting the news isn't doing something. It just feels like it.
videoIdeas.rationale: My top post ever (6,134 views) was about the necessity of protest and taking action, and my June/July posts hammer 'focus on what's dire'. My audience clearly responds to the action-vs-noise theme. Reframing it as a mindset lesson makes it repeatable content instead of a one-off reaction, and it's authentically mine.
videoIdeas.script:
Reposting the news isn't doing something. It just feels like it.

We've confused emotion with effort. You feel angry, you feel heartbroken, you share the post, you feel like you've contributed. You haven't. You've just moved the feeling around.

And the algorithm loves it, because outrage keeps you on the app instead of off it doing something that costs you.

Ask yourself honestly — in the last month, what did your anger actually produce? A donation? A boycott you kept? A skill you're building so you're useful later? Or just a camera roll full of screenshots?

The Ummah doesn't need more people who feel strongly. It needs more people who do something small and consistent. Pick one thing. Do it quietly. That's worth more than a thousand reposts.

visuals.setting: Direct-to-camera, plain background, serious and steady. No smiling — this is the sharp older brother telling you a hard truth. Tight mid-shot.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'feeling angry ≠ doing something' over a close, still shot of your face.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open holding up a phone showing a share button, 'this isn't it'
Pattern interrupt: 'I'm going to annoy some of you with this one'
On-screen counter/text listing 'shared, cried, moved on' getting crossed out

videoIdeas.title: The version of you at home
videoIdeas.hook: The you at home is the real you. Everything else is marketing.
videoIdeas.rationale: @doctordaanish's biggest non-viral hits were both about character at home (193k, and the family patience one). It's a proven emotional angle in this exact niche. It maps to my leadership pillar via the Prophetic 'best of you is best to their family' hadith — and I've already posted hadith-based content (455-463 views) that lands well on engagement ratio.
videoIdeas.script:
The you at home is the real you. Everything else is marketing.

It's easy to be patient in public. Easy to be generous when people are watching. The mask holds for a couple of hours. The test is what happens when you walk through your own front door tired and no one's filming.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said the best of you are the best to their families. Not the best on a stage. Not the best with strangers. Their families.

Because your family sees the version you don't post. The short temper, the ignored questions, the phone in your hand while someone's talking to you.

You want to know if you're actually the leader you think you are? Don't ask your followers. Ask the people who live with you. Their answer is the honest one.

visuals.setting: Warmer, softer setting — home environment, lamp light, relaxed clothing. Calmer and more personal than the leadership 'framework' videos. Sit down like you're having a real conversation.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'ask the people who live with you' held while you speak the opening line softly.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open: 'your followers can't tell you if you're a good person'
Pattern interrupt — start with a fake compliment then undercut it: 'you're so patient. in public.'
Text punchline on final frame: 'the version you don't post'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your all-time top post at 6,134 views — nearly double your next best. The hook ('Can't believe we're still discussing the necessity of protests in 2026') is dated, specific and takes an immediate side, which is why it travelled. Taking a clear stance on a live topic is your distribution engine.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 211 likes but only 15 comments — for a post this divisive that comment count is low, meaning it got shared/viewed more than it sparked debate. End with a direct question or a challenge ('tell me why I'm wrong') to convert those views into comments, which pushes reach further.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 2,106 views with a 138-like ratio (6.5%) — your strongest like-to-view rate in the top tier. The UAE 'Hijrah bros' angle is sharp, specific, and names a real trend people recognise. This is your voice at its best: blunt, targeted, articulate.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 5 comments despite the strong likes — the take is so complete it leaves nothing to argue about. Leave one deliberate open loop or ask 'am I being unfair here?' to pull out the counter-arguments. Also the caption cuts off mid-sentence ('brag ab') — tighten it so the hook lands fully in-feed.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 827 views but 24 comments — the highest comment-to-view ratio in your whole set. 'Don't let sectarianism blind you' hits a nerve that forces people to respond. You've found a topic your audience will actually argue under, which is gold for reach.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 42 likes against those 24 comments suggests the comments skew combative rather than supportive — fine, but the view count stayed low. The caption is a bare statement; add a line of actual argument or a hadith to give the algorithm text to work with and give agreeing viewers a reason to like and share, not just fight.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your best true-pillar content: 'influence before character / Al-Qawi wal-Ameen' pulled 58 likes on 508 views — an 11% like rate, far above your commentary posts. This proves your leadership pillar resonates hard with the people it reaches. The line-broken, punchy caption format reads well.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 508 views is low because it lacks a controversy hook to trigger distribution. Front-load a blunter opening line ('everyone wants to be followed, nobody wants to be trustworthy') instead of the softer 'We often chase influence.' Marry your leadership substance to your commentary-style hooks and this format could break out.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 883 views shows the topic still reaches. You're clearly trying to draw a real distinction (trivialising vs having fun) which is thoughtful and on-brand.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments — a red flag. The caption is abstract and references a previous video ('I've already spoken about this'), so new viewers have no entry point and nothing to react to. Make each post self-contained, lead with the concrete example not the abstract principle, and close with a question. Nuanced points need sharper hooks or they die in the feed.
